data.title: Taking Action on AMD, Alphabet and Meta After Steep Nasdaq Selloff
data.description:
The Nasdaq Composite had its worst day in 19 months, losing over 5.5% on Thursday. The tech-heavy index closed below its 200-day moving average (red) for the first time in over six months. 

On the positive side, the selloff was orderly, a sign that market participants aren’t panicking. On the negative side is the fact that the major indexes all closed at or near their lows. The absence of a sustained rally off the lows could be taken as a sign that further selling is likely. 

Before that happens, the index could bounce from here, as Thursday’s close (point B) is near in price to the index’s six-month low (point A). If that bounce occurs, investors should use it to further lighten up on tech, especially anything related to artificial intelligence and data centers.

AMD in Full Retreat

Shares of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell by 17.26%. AMD is now down 37% since setting an all-time high just one month ago. Amazingly, this stock is still up by over 80% year-to-date. 

AMD closed beneath its 200-day moving average (red) for the first time this year. The selloff occurred on the stock’s heaviest volume since May. The high volume, plus the fact that the stock closed at its low of the day, indicates that any rally from this point is likely to be short-lived.

AMD soared after our initial recommendation to buy at $105. After reducing our shares by half late last year, and cutting the remainder by half again this past summer, we closed the final 25% of our AMD position Thursday.

We’ve now completely exited the AI chip sector, with the exception of a miniature 25% position in Nvidia (NVDA). 

A Meta Headache

We also cast off our recently opened position in Meta Platforms (META) for a loss of about 4%. Meta could be headed for $520 (black horizontal line). The stock bounced sharply from that area in March for a gain of 32% (point A), and again in August for a gain of 47% (point B). If we can get Meta in the $520 area, we’ll consider buying the stock again.

Alphabet City

We’re still holding Alphabet (GOOGL), another recent purchase, because that stock has held up very well under pressure. Alphabet continues to hold above a major support level (black line) that has generated two strong bounces (points A and B).

Alphabet demonstrated impressive strength during Thursday’s selloff, falling by less than 2%. If the market bounces from here, Alphabet could fly. On the other hand, if the parent company of Google and YouTube breaks below support, we won’t hesitate to cut our losses. 

Stalwart Staples

One encouraging aspect of Thursday’s price action was the relative strength of the consumer staples sector. The State Street Consumer Staples ETF (XLY) actually gapped higher at the open, and closed lower by less than 1% in a very red market.

Kimberly-Clark (KMB) gained 1.5% for the day. Shares of the personal care and hygiene products company have now gained 12% since we recommended the stock in September (arrow).

We’ll continue to move away from tech and allocate more funds toward consumer-focused names like Kimberly-Clark.

data.title: ‘Not Even Close,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Memory chips had been the market’s favorite story for most of the year, although cracks had started to show recently, and on Thursday that story fell apart. Democrats’ midterm sweep raised fears of a slowdown in the data center build-out, investors dumped anything tied to AI, and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) took one of the worst hits.

The selling was very heavy indeed. Micron fell 17.5%, its biggest one-day drop in more than a year. The Nasdaq had its worst day in 19 months and fell into a correction. Along with other tech names, the stock is pushing higher today, although it now trades 43% below its June peak.

A top investor going by the moniker of Cash Flow Venue (CFV), a long-time follower of the company, has taken a new look at what’s going on.

The investor’s main point is that memory no longer has to follow the old boom-and-bust pattern. Each new phase of AI uses much more of it than the one before, whether that’s generative tools, autonomous agents, or robots in the physical world. Others in the industry agree. SK hynix’s CEO, Kwak Noh-Jung, has said the memory shortage could continue to the end of 2030, and Micron expects supply to stay tight through fiscal 2027 and 2028. CFV, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, also points to how much the big cloud companies are willing to spend. Amazon put $211 billion into property and equipment over the trailing 12 months, which pushed its free cash flow to negative $42 billion. In the investor’s view, companies spending like that are not about to stop buying memory.

So far, the numbers have kept up with the story. Fourth-quarter revenue came in at $54.2 billion, up 379% year over year, and adjusted EPS jumped to $33.42 from $3.03 a year earlier. The operating margin for the quarter was 82%, ahead of even SK hynix, which posted 76% in its latest quarter. Management expects the next quarter to be bigger still, guiding for revenue of about $61.5 billion and adjusted EPS of around $38.

After Thursday’s sell-off, Micron traded at under 4 times forward earnings, the cheapest of 10 U.S. chip stocks in a recent screen, and at 5.6 times trailing 12-month sales, compared with 3.2 times for the S&P 500. CFV says that is a low price for a company growing faster than almost any other chipmaker.

The 5-star investor does see risks. If the shortage ends early, Micron would lose much of its pricing power, and its margins would follow. Politics could also get in the way, since Democratic lawmakers want data center operators to pay more of the cost of new power infrastructure. CFV doesn’t expect either risk to hit soon, because the biggest tech companies can handle several years of weak cash flow if they have to.

Bottom line, Cash Flow Venue expects large gains over the long run and is sticking with a Strong Buy rating on Micron. (To watch Cash Flow Venue’s track record, click here)

Hardly any Street analysts have a problem with that assessment. Based on 28 Buys vs. 1 Hold, the consensus view is that this stock is a Strong Buy. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 136.5%, given the average price target clocks in at $1,621.67. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Get Out of Rocket Lab Stock While You Can, Says Investor Ahead of Earnings
data.description:
When a stock loses most of its value in a few months, it usually starts to look like a bargain. Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) is putting that idea to the test. A delayed debut for the Neutron rocket, a broad tech sell-off and new worries about defense budgets after Democrats’ midterm wins have all hit the shares, and Thursday brought another hard fall.

Despite today’s 11% bounce, the stock has now lost around 66% since its record close in late May, but if you think that means the huge pullback makes the stock an appealing choice for bottom feeders, investor Lee Bailey would like a word.

Ahead of the company’s third-quarter report on Monday (November 9), Bailey isn’t convinced the sell-off has gone far enough.

That’s not to say the investor doubts Rocket Lab is a real business. Electron, its small-satellite rocket, flies on a regular basis for customers who pay for it, which is more than most launch startups can say. Most of the money, however, comes from Space Systems, the unit that builds satellites and components. It made up about 81% of second-quarter revenue, as total sales jumped 62% year over year to $234.1 million.

Demand isn’t the issue either, with backlog reaching $2.36 billion at the end of June. Bailey’s concern is that a big order book doesn’t automatically turn into profit. Most of the business is spacecraft work, and Space Systems earns a gross margin of roughly 35%, below the 43% or so the launch side makes. Big contracts can also go wrong, and Rocket Lab has already disclosed delays and possible penalties on a 17-spacecraft program it’s building for Canada’s MDA.

Neutron is the next question mark. Management has pointed to pricing of $50 million to $55 million per mission, but the first flight has slipped to 2027. In the investor’s view, a maiden launch tells you very little about reuse, turnaround costs or demand, and SpaceX already competes for the same customers.

He likes the pending Iridium deal for its steady service revenue. Satellites wear out, though. Merger proxy forecasts show Iridium’s unlevered free cash flow at $529 million in 2030, then turning negative the following year as replacement spending kicks in. Rocket Lab has also issued about 29.3 million new shares to raise $1.94 billion and used $134.4 million in operating cash in the first half.

Then there’s valuation, the area where Bailey really gets stuck. He puts fair value at about $20 a share, so at ~$51, the stock trades at more than two and a half times what he thinks it’s worth. His $20 already sits above his base-case estimate of $14, because he gives some credit for Neutron and Rocket Lab’s technology. Even his most optimistic scenario, which needs Rocket Lab to generate roughly $4.4 billion in free cash flow in 2040, comes out at about $41, still below the share price.

So, Bailey rates the stock a Strong Sell and would get out before Monday’s report. (To watch Bailey’s track record, click here)

That said, none of the Street’s analysts think that’s a good idea. In fact, based on 15 Buys and 3 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus view. At $99.19, the average price target implies shares will gain 94% over the one-year timeframe. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: SanDisk Stock’s (SNDK) Sell-Off Is a Gift Worth Taking
data.description:
SanDisk (SNDK) stock’s recent sell-off looks like a gift from the market that is worth taking. After an explosive rally, the NAND memory chipmaker was hit hard by fears of slowing prices, doubts about the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and risks to U.S. data center expansion.

Yet there’s something that catches my eye. While SanDisk shares have been in a downward spiral, margins remain extraordinary, and cash flow generation is still strong.

With long-term contracts making the business more predictable and the stock trading at just 7x what I consider normalized free cash flow (FCF), I see the recent sell-off as a buying opportunity. That’s even though the stock remains at the mercy of broader market sentiment toward AI.

What Went Wrong with SanDisk?

Although SanDisk has already lost more than 60% of its market value since its June highs, the memory chip company remains second only to Moderna (MRNA) in year-to-date returns among S&P 500 (SPX) stocks, with shares still up roughly 240% as of this writing.

However, to understand SanDisk’s recent loss of momentum, let’s break it down into three parts.

The first phase came between June and July, when enthusiasm for AI-related memory stocks began to cool. While SanDisk’s explosive performance in the first half of 2026 was driven by rising NAND prices and AI demand, investors soon began to question whether the market had already priced in the best possible results. Investors also rotated into other tech sectors, such as software, which had been severely punished.

Then came October. Toward the end of the month, SanDisk reported excellent results but faced a terrible market reaction. Its $11 billion in revenue, up 378% year-over-year, and non-GAAP gross margin of 85.1% weren’t enough to prevent a 13.5% drop on October 30.

The biggest warning came from Japanese rival Kioxia (JP:285A), a major flash memory and SSD maker. Sequential growth in average NAND prices slowed from roughly 70% in the previous quarter to the mid-20% range in September. Prices were still rising, but much more slowly, suggesting SanDisk could eventually face a similar slowdown.

Another Hammer Blow from Washington

Then came another hammer blow in early November, as investors grew more wary of AI-related risks following the Democrats’ victories in the Senate and House. On November 5, SNDK lost another 22.3%, alongside heavy selling pressure on peers such as Micron (MU) and Western Digital (WDC).

The Democrats’ victories also raised concerns about future data center expansion. After all, several candidates who pushed for restrictions on new projects won their races. This includes the Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas. Several towns in Ohio also voted to block or restrict new data center projects.

That’s a big deal. According to Bloomberg, roughly 40% of planned U.S. data center capacity is in states where newly elected leaders have called for pauses or restrictions. Texas, Ohio, and Georgia are among the key states facing this uncertainty.

SanDisk’s Margins Tell a Different Story

Yet here’s a bullish take. Despite all the recent headwinds, mostly macro-related, SanDisk’s gross margins have risen by more than 55 percentage points in just one year. Meanwhile, the stock is 63.5% below its peak.

This shows just how tight memory supply has been and how strong demand has become. Nothing new here, of course. Yet what’s interesting is that the market is already pricing in a normalization of these conditions. SanDisk still projects a non-GAAP gross margin of 84.5% to 85.5% for Q2 FY27. So there’s no sign of a near-term margin reversal.

Another factor working in SanDisk’s favor is that the biggest weakness in its investment thesis, the cyclical nature of the memory business, may be becoming less of a concern.

The company has been trying to reduce its exposure to spot NAND prices by shifting toward long-term contracts, known as New Business Models (NBMs). These contracts already cover about half of its projected bits for FY2027 and two-thirds for FY2028. They also carry $93.9 billion in minimum contracted revenue at floor prices and $16.5 billion in financial guarantees. Their weighted average term exceeds four years.

The key point is that these agreements don’t eliminate cyclical risk. However, they arguably offer more protection than relying solely on market prices, thanks to a mix of fixed and variable pricing.

So the big question for SanDisk’s thesis is whether the market will continue to value it as a traditional NAND manufacturer, despite its changing business model.

How Much of SanDisk’s Cash Flow Can Last?

Another piece of the puzzle is that even if these NBMs make SanDisk’s margins more predictable and potentially earn it a valuation premium, that doesn’t mean today’s profitability is sustainable. For investors trying to figure out whether the stock is genuinely cheap after such a massive sell-off, what ultimately matters is how much of that profitability turns into recurring free cash flow.

The latest numbers are nothing short of impressive. SanDisk generated $5.7 billion in adjusted FCF in Q1 FY27, up from $5 billion in the previous quarter and just $448 million a year earlier. Its adjusted FCF margin reached 51.6%, although that was down from 56.2% in the previous quarter.

Annualizing the latest quarter would imply nearly $23 billion in FCF. Of course, assuming that level can last indefinitely makes little sense for a cyclical business.

So, rather than extrapolating peak profitability, I think it makes more sense to test what SanDisk could generate under more conservative FCF margin assumptions.

What Would It Take to Revisit All-Time Highs?

At roughly $851.94 per share, SanDisk has a market cap of just under $121 billion. Its forward P/E of around 3.7x looks incredibly cheap. Yet for a cyclical business, normalized FCF offers a better perspective. Based on roughly $14 billion in adjusted FCF over the past 12 months, the stock currently trades at just 8.7x FCF.

Consensus estimates point to roughly $49.56 billion in FY27 revenue. At a 35% FCF margin, that would translate into about $17.3 billion in annual cash generation. That puts SanDisk at roughly 7x normalized FCF today. A re-rating to 10x would imply a valuation of around $173 billion, or roughly 43% upside from current levels.

What would it take to revisit its June high of $2,335? At 15x FCF, SanDisk would need to sustain around $22.2 billion in annual FCF. That implies a margin of roughly 45% on the same revenue base.

That’s not entirely unrealistic, considering management’s long-term targets. Still, Wall Street would need to stop treating SanDisk’s extraordinary cash generation as a temporary windfall from peak NAND prices. That’s a much tougher hurdle than delivering another blowout quarter.

Is SNDK a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Wall Street’s SNDK forecast remains very bullish, with analysts giving the stock an overall Strong Buy consensus rating. Of the 18 ratings issued over the past three months, 15 are Buy and only three are Hold. Even more striking is the average SanDisk price target of $2,080.59, which implies a 144% upside from current levels.

The Discount Looks Too Steep

To me, a return to 10x normalized FCF looks quite reasonable for SNDK. It wouldn’t require another surge in NAND prices or a return to today’s 50%-plus FCF margins. My base case already assumes a much more modest 35% margin.

More importantly, SanDisk’s long-term contracts should give investors better visibility into future cash generation, something a cyclical business typically lacks.

If the company can prove these agreements help protect margins as NAND prices cool, I see little reason for the market to keep valuing it at just 7x normalized FCF. That’s why I see the recent sell-off as a buying opportunity, rather than a warning to stay away.

data.title: ‘Lost in Space,’ Says Top Investor About SpaceX Stock
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) arrived on the market as the biggest IPO in history, priced as if it already owned the future of space travel, internet access and AI. Five months on, much of that excitement has worn off. The selling picked up this week after Democrats swept the midterms, clouding the outlook for a possible Tesla merger and for Washington’s attitude toward Elon Musk’s businesses. Despite today’s rebound, the shares remain below their $135 IPO price.

The slide comes even though SpaceX’s third quarter beat Wall Street’s estimates on both the top and bottom lines.

However, a top investor using the pseudonym The Value Portfolio (TVP) thinks the headline figures paint a kinder picture than the business deserves. Based on third-quarter operating income of $2.79 billion, the investor puts SpaceX at roughly 180x earnings, meaning profits would need to grow almost tenfold to match the S&P 500’s multiple. Capital spending, meanwhile, is running at well over $65 billion a year.

The launch business is TVP’s first worry. Space segment revenue rose only about 2% year over year in the first nine months, slower than inflation, and the unit’s adjusted EBITDA swung to a loss. In the investor’s view, Starlink is effectively keeping the launch side afloat.

Connectivity is the bright spot, with nine-month revenue up more than 50% and operating income up about two-thirds. Still, the push into cellular, backed by a $17 billion deal for EchoStar spectrum, would require a ground network, since satellites can’t reach indoors. That’s hardly new, TVP argues, and AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile have already teamed up to pool spectrum for satellite service, with Amazon Leo also in the mix.

TVP, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, also flags SpaceX’s handling of Ukraine. In October, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered a slowdown of a military Starlink service that Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and to keep its drones connected, and Musk later acknowledged the throttling. For TVP, the lesson for governments is to own their networks. Ukraine has since signed a letter of intent with Finland’s Nokia and ICEYE to build its own system.

TVP is just as doubtful about the AI unit. Much of its revenue comes from renting out compute, including Anthropic’s $1.25 billion-a-month contract, which the investor reads as a sign of weak demand for Grok. The segment lost more than $3 billion over nine months, even as SpaceX put $16.4 billion of capex into it in the third quarter alone.

The 5-star investor doubts that money will earn outsized returns. Grok’s newest model sits 43rd on LMArena’s text leaderboard, and it goes up against deep-pocketed players like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, plus free open-source options such as Kimi. Unlike Amazon and Google, SpaceX also doesn’t have its own custom chips to keep costs down. On top of that, TVP argues that adjusted EBITDA flatters SpaceX by excluding stock-based compensation, a recurring cost that dilutes shareholders.

Put together, The Value Portfolio rates the stock a Strong Sell. (To watch The Value Portfolio’s track record, click here)

However, only 1 Street analyst agrees with that bearish sentiment. Elsewhere, an additional 28 Buys and 5 Holds all add up to a Strong Buy consensus rating. Meanwhile, the $253.57 average price target implies shares will gain 94% over the one-year timeframe. (See SPCX stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Where’s the Cash?’ Asks Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) spent last week selling investors on a bold long-term vision, then asked them to help pay for it. The pitch landed well at first, and the shares rallied on the company’s Investor Day. The mood turned once Oracle went to the market for its latest round of funding, and the stock has since slipped back toward the bottom of its range for the past year, with shares down 41% year to date.

The raise came to $20 billion, split evenly between new shares and senior notes, with the stock priced at $116 apiece. It arrived just five days after management set a fiscal 2030 revenue target of $225 billion or more, which works out to compound annual growth above 35% from fiscal 2026. Oracle also expects free cash flow to turn positive late in fiscal 2028 and reach at least $30 billion the following year. At the same event, it capped new capital-market funding through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion. It used up that limit almost immediately.

A 5-star investor using the moniker The Value Investor (TVI) thinks the market has good reason to stay wary. TVI acknowledges that the business keeps growing. In the fiscal first quarter (August quarter), revenue rose 30% year over year to $19.3 billion, driven by a 121% jump in cloud infrastructure sales to $7.4 billion. Profits grew faster still, with GAAP EPS up 55% to $1.56, and remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion.

According to TVI, cash is where things get uncomfortable. Capital spending hit $28.5 billion in the quarter, which kept free cash flow negative, and the investor puts net debt near $100 billion. There are some bright spots. Customer prepayments are lowering the actual cost of the build-out, and with quarterly EBITDA of around $10 billion, TVI sees the debt as manageable for now. Meanwhile, the legacy software business shrank 3% YoY.

The stock now trades at roughly 5x sales and about 15x earnings, and TVI thinks the discount is deserved. Oracle has no AI models of its own and no consumer business to spread its spending across. Its core operation is also smaller and less cash-generative than those of its hyperscale rivals. On top of that, it began this spending cycle with plenty of debt already on the books. The investor also points to setbacks at some major projects and says Oracle co-founder and chairman Larry Ellison’s attention seems to be drifting toward media deals.

Now that investors are separating AI winners from losers instead of buying the whole group, TVI puts Oracle in the weaker camp. The new equity helps, but the investor sees it as small next to Oracle’s funding needs, especially with the core business under strain. For now, TVI doesn’t see the stock as a clear buy.

Thus, TVI rates the stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch The Value Investor’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 4 analysts are also on the fence, although an additional 28 Buys and 1 Sell all add up to a Strong Buy consensus view. The forecast calls for one-year gains of 107%, considering the average target stands at $242.50. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Guilt by Association,’ Says Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) spent the first half of the year as the poster child for the AI memory boom. On Thursday, it became the poster child for the AI hangover. The flash memory maker led a brutal rout in chip stocks as investors, rattled by the Democrats’ midterm sweep and the prospect of new limits on data-center construction, dumped anything tied to the AI buildout. This morning, bargain hunters are back and the shares are bouncing hard in premarket trading.

The damage was severe. Sandisk closed Thursday down 22%, the Nasdaq-100 suffered its worst day since April 2025, and the stock now sits 62% below its peak. Early Friday, it is up more than 10%.

Investor Kucheriavyi, who had previously been on the sidelines, thinks the market is punishing the wrong thing. In the investor’s view, the selloff is about nerves over AI spending, not about anything breaking at the company.

Kucheriavyi points to the latest quarter as evidence. Revenue reached $11.03 billion, up 378% year over year, while adjusted EPS of $49.51 cleared the top of management’s $44 to $46 range. Data-center sales did the heavy lifting, jumping 61% from the prior quarter to $4.8 billion. For Q2, management guided revenue to $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion and expects prices to edge up modestly through the fiscal year.

What stands out most to the investor is visibility, which memory makers rarely get. Roughly half of Sandisk’s fiscal 2027 bits and two-thirds of fiscal 2028 bits are already locked into long-term agreements, and management says customer commitments run past 2030. Partner Kioxia has reportedly said its 2027 capacity is spoken for, and TrendForce expects NAND contract prices to rise another 15% to 20% this quarter.

Cash isn’t a problem either. Sandisk generated $5.7 billion in adjusted free cash flow, spent $5 billion on buybacks, and ended the quarter with $5.1 billion in cash and no debt. Kucheriavyi argues that buybacks at this pace could help support the shares even if AI sentiment stays sour.

On valuation, the investor reran a discounted cash flow model with much tamer inputs, including 145% revenue growth in fiscal 2027 and a 70% EBIT margin, and still found the stock trading well below fair value. The multiples point the same way. As of Thursday’s close, Sandisk had a market cap of about $115 billion and traded at a trailing P/E near 6.5, against a five-year median above 22.

The risks haven’t gone away. Memory is still a cyclical business, consumer revenue fell 29% QoQ, and management admits fiscal Q3 is usually the softest quarter. Kioxia’s flat forecast for the current quarter, which it tied to currency effects, has also raised fears that NAND prices are close to peaking. If pricing stalls, the stock could keep lagging even when results beat.

Even so, Kucheriavyi has turned bullish and sees the crash as a “golden opportunity” for long-term investors.

As such, the investor has upgraded SNDK’s rating from Hold (i.e., Neutral) to Buy. (To watch Kucheriavyi’s track record, click here)

Most on the Street wholeheartedly agree. Based on a mix of 15 Buys and 3 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $2,080.59, the average price target offers 12-month upside of 158%. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: Intel Stock’s (INTC) Deep Sell-Off Shows Signs of an Overreaction
data.description:
Intel Corporation (INTC) stock’s deep sell-off shows signs of an overreaction, in my view, as the market may be overlooking the progress the chipmaker has made in its recovery. Since its June peak, the company’s market capitalization has fallen by more than half. In late October, shares cratered nearly 30% in a single session after the company issued disappointing fourth-quarter guidance. The fear now is that its recovery could take much longer than expected.

Yet isn’t there some market overreaction? Despite the weak guidance, Intel delivered a solid third quarter, with 78% growth in its data center segment and significant improvements in manufacturing efficiency.

Risks remain, particularly the foundry business’s heavy losses, ongoing production constraints, and massive capital spending that continues to weigh on free cash flow (FCF). Still, I see a buying opportunity after the sell-off, at the current price of $52.25. Projected 2028 adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.99 valued at a five-year average forward P/E of 27x supports an $80.73 price target, implying potential upside of 55%.

The Sell-Off Didn’t Come Out of Nowhere

Intel’s recent sell-off didn’t happen without reason. After it released its third-quarter results on October 29, the semiconductor giant’s shares plunged a staggering 28.6% in a single trading session on October 30.

Essentially, Intel provided guidance that fell well short of expectations. While Wall Street analysts projected Q4 revenue of about $17 billion, Intel’s management guided to just $15 billion to $16 billion. Meanwhile, adjusted EPS guidance of $0.25 came in well below Wall Street’s expectations of $0.44.

As if that weren’t bad enough, management warned of production constraints, prolonged weakness in the PC market, and difficulties generating FCF in 2026. In fact, FCF was negative $1.47 billion over the last 12 months.

A Strong Quarter, but a Cloudy Outlook

At the same time, it’s worth pointing out that the problem wasn’t necessarily the Q3 results themselves, which, frankly, were good and even quite strong in some respects. For example, revenue and adjusted EPS rose 21% and 126%, respectively, year-over-year. Adjusted gross margin also reached 44%, up 4.1 percentage points.

The bigger concern is the possibility that Wall Street may need to revise its 2027 and 2028 projections downward. In fact, over the last three months, 2027 revenue estimates have been trimmed by roughly 3% to $69.27 billion, implying 12% year-over-year growth. Surprisingly, though, 2028 revenue estimates have actually been revised upward by nearly 2% over the same period. Consensus now points to $83.7 billion, implying 20.9% annual growth.

Intel’s Data Center Segment Tells a Different Story

To determine whether this sell-off reflects temporary problems or a permanent deterioration in the business, look at Intel’s data center business.

In Q3, revenue from the Data Center and AI segment reached $7.3 billion, up 78% year-over-year. Meanwhile, Client Computing revenue reached $8.1 billion, representing a 5% year-over-year decline.

Yet the devil is in the details. The Data Center & AI segment generated $3.04 billion in operating profit in Q3, compared to just $964 million a year earlier. In other words, operating profit more than tripled. This supports a key argument that Intel appears to be moving away from relying so heavily on the traditional PC market to drive growth. Also, its server business is rapidly becoming a much more important driver of revenue and profitability.

A Better Problem to Have

What’s most interesting is that this data center growth didn’t come simply from selling more processors. According to Intel, average selling prices (ASPs) for server chips rose an impressive 54% in Q3, while volume grew 10%. Much of the ASP increase came from a more favorable mix of premium products, rather than just price hikes. This helps explain why the segment’s operating profit grew so much faster than revenue.

There’s another detail I find particularly bullish. Demand continues to outpace production capacity. Intel also reported growth among hyperscalers, enterprise customers, and new cloud providers, despite ongoing supply constraints. Management expects these constraints to persist through 2027 and into 2028. Meanwhile, it projects annual growth of more than 30% in industry-wide server CPU volumes in both 2026 and 2027.

In other words, Intel’s problem in this business seems to be more about its ability to meet demand than a lack of it. That, in my view, is a much healthier problem to have.

The Foundry Bet Is Starting to Pay Off for Intel

In addition to data centers, Intel’s foundry business is another key part of its turnaround strategy. The goal is to compete with TSMC (TSM) in advanced semiconductor manufacturing. Recent progress has been encouraging, too. In Q3, Intel reported that manufacturing costs for its 18A process had fallen by roughly 40% since Q1, thanks to better yields and improved production efficiency.

This is already a significant step forward, although there’s still much to prove. Intel Foundry reported $6.7 billion in revenue for the quarter, but only $411 million came from external customers. Its operating loss also remained substantial at $1.85 billion, although that was down from $2.32 billion a year earlier.

This is precisely where Intel’s valuation starts to make sense. Following Q3, the sell-side consensus calls for adjusted EPS of $2.99 in 2028. As a benchmark, I use Intel’s own five-year average forward P/E of 27x, which I believe is reasonable if the turnaround stays on track. Applying that multiple to projected earnings gives me a price target of approximately $80.73 per share, or 55% upside from the current $52.25 over the next 12 months.

Is INTC a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Following Q3, some analysts downgraded Intel shares, adding to Wall Street’s skepticism. According to TipRanks, the INTC forecast still shows an overall Hold consensus. Of the 33 analyst ratings issued over the past three months, only seven are Buy, while 25 are Hold and one is Sell. Interestingly, the average Intel price target stands at $91.62, which, despite the skepticism, still implies a massive 75.35% upside from current levels.

Intel’s Turnaround Is Still Worth Betting On

Intel’s turnaround is far from a done deal, and its stock remains highly volatile. However, there’s a big difference between a company struggling to find demand and one struggling to keep up with it. Stronger server sales, less dependence on PCs, improving margins, and progress in the foundry business suggest the recovery is gaining traction.

Of course, the road ahead remains bumpy, with heavy capital spending, foundry losses, and production constraints. Still, at current price levels, I see these headwinds as more related to capacity than weak demand, making the recent sell-off an attractive buying opportunity and supporting my bullish stance on INTC.

data.title: Will Superintelligence Spending Sink Meta Stock (META)?
data.description:
Meta (META) stock could come under further pressure as investors grow more concerned about the company’s aggressive superintelligence spending. Recent earnings results from its peers offer a warning. Alphabet (GOOGL) shares plunged after the company missed Q3 earnings expectations and reported negative free cash flow. Amazon (AMZN) also fell short of Wall Street’s earnings estimates of $1.96, reporting $1.89 earnings per share (EPS). With Meta committing billions to its superintelligence buildout and with the path to payoff remaining unclear, I expect the spending burden to weigh on its shares through year-end, keeping me bearish.

The social media giant behind Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Muse has seen its stock grow at a 21.4% average compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) since 2019. However, the market’s enthusiasm for the superintelligence trade is waning despite Meta’s consistently strong balance sheet and performance. 

The bulls still have some ammunition, though. September’s release of its much-hyped agentic app, Muse, topped Apple’s (AAPL) App Store charts, boosting Meta’s share price to $779, a 30% bump for the month. Yet the stock has since retreated, up only about 1% from where it started in September. Additionally, S&P Global Ratings (SPGI) has readjusted Meta’s credit standing, citing negative cash flow and capex concerns. 

Where Is Meta Spending?

Meta’s 2026 total capex — driven primarily by its superintelligence buildout — is expected to reach $135 billion to $145 billion, following billions spent in 2024 and 2025. Looking ahead, S&P Global Ratings recently forecast Meta’s 2027 and 2028 capex spending will rise to $225 billion and $252 billion, respectively. This forecast has prompted S&P to adjust its AA- rating outlook from Positive to Negative

Meta’s Reality Labs division and settling lawsuits have also been a drag on financial performance. Reality Labs has launched popular Virtual Reality headsets and Smart Glasses. Meta’s upcoming gadget, the Muse Charm, could also be a holiday hit. So what’s the drag? Reality Labs continues to lose billions quarterly while revenue is only a few hundred million dollars. Not to mention the ongoing court cases that could make Meta liable for tens of billions of dollars. 

Fast Growth, but Only in One Segment

Meta’s $200.97 billion in revenue is more than double what it was in 2020. Most investors are not concerned about the company’s ability to grow revenue. 

Most investors are concerned about Meta’s ability to diversify its revenue. Advertising accounts for 97.6% of Meta’s revenue. Meta is an incredibly rich company that continues to spend an insane amount of money on products that generate very little revenue. On a positive note, it shows management’s willingness to take risks.

How Macroeconomic Factors Will Affect Superintelligence Spending 

Macroeconomic factors will have an increasingly bigger impact on stock valuations until after the first half of 2027. Rising interest rates will make the cost of borrowing more expensive, and voter discontent over data centers swept through the U.S. midterms. One positive boost will come in the form of an Anthropic (ANT) initial public offering (IPO) in November, but some pessimism is showing in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) names, neoclouds, and power equipment makers. 

For example, neoclouds are feeling the heat after Democrats won both houses of Congress the day after the midterms. Rising energy prices and high water usage have been blamed on data centers. Stock prices for Coreweave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS), and Iren (IREN) were down almost double digits in the two days following the election. Democratic Party wins have also pushed down power equipment makers’ share prices, with names GE Vernova (GEV), Siemens Energy (SMEGF), and Caterpillar (CAT) dipping in the short term. Anti-data center sentiment prompted Goldman Sachs (GS) to publish a report saying 45% of U.S. data center projects could be at risk because of politics.

Advertising Revenue Masks Risks to Valuation

Meta’s strong Q3 year-over-year revenue growth of 26% beat Wall Street’s estimates, with over 97% of this revenue coming from advertising. Estimated Q3 EPS was $6.54, with reported EPS coming in at $3.83. The low reported number reflects a substantial payment to settle a lawsuit, giving bulls justification for focusing on the top line. Meta’s P/E of 20.78x is low compared with its Mag 7 counterparts.

Investors should monitor how Meta finances its superintelligence buildout, including its recent $20 billion bond sale and corporate actions like its planned 2-for-1 stock split in January 2027. With negative free cash flow and escalating spending, this could weaken the balance sheet and, consequently, the share price.

The -23.42 Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) at a one-day interval has triggered a Buy score according to Technical Analysis, even while most Moving Averages show Sell. The MACD indicates recent volatility may have pushed META into oversold territory. Conversely, the Cboe Global Markets (CBOE) Volatility Index jumped to over 23 on November 5. This suggests market volatility has been unpredictable because of the superintelligence trade, and Meta’s negative Moving Averages support that view. 

Analyst Forecast on META 

Of the 43 analysts covering META, 37 rate it a Buy, six rate it a Hold, and zero rate it a Sell. The average 12-month price target of $859.32 implies a 42.02% upside from its last closing price of $605.08.

Truist Financial analyst Youssef Squali reiterated his Buy and raised his META price target from $763 to $1,000 per share. 

Conclusion: Sour Public Sentiment Outweighs Benefits

Whether the negative public sentiment surrounding data center construction is warranted or not matters little in the near term, as investors will need time to assess potential new regulations. While the broader economic benefits of AI infrastructure outweigh short-term voter discontent, rising borrowing costs will add further pressure as the Fed begins its rate-hiking cycle. With trillions in planned industry spending and an uncertain timeline for profitable superintelligence monetization, Meta’s shareholder value could remain compressed over the next few quarters.

data.title: Caterpillar Stock’s (CAT) Sell-Off Has Gone Too Far. Here’s Why
data.description:
Caterpillar (CAT) stock’s sell-off looks overdone, in my view, especially as customers keep filling its order book. The industrial equipment manufacturer is about 47% below its 52-week high. Political concerns now add to anxieties about artificial intelligence (AI) spending.

Yet CEO Joe Creed says “we have line of sight past the backlog.” That backlog stands at $78.1 billion. My CAT stock forecast remains bullish after its massive sell-off because Caterpillar can benefit from years of infrastructure investment, with demand extending well beyond data centers.

Caterpillar’s Q3 Shows Exceptional Execution

Caterpillar’s Q3 showed exceptional execution despite the market’s disappointment. Sales rose 17% to $20.7 billion. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) increased to $7.20 from $4.95 year-over-year. Adjusted operating margin expanded to 20.6%, against 17.5% last year.

Enterprise operating cash flow reached $4.4 billion. Higher shipments to end users drove most of the volume growth, while favorable pricing contributed $663 million.

However, Power & Energy stood out for me. Sales increased 18% to $8.8 billion, while segment profit jumped 31%. Turbines and large reciprocating engines serving data centers helped drive growth. The faster profit increase shows how greater output can improve earnings. Power-generation sales to end users grew 75%, showing demand beyond factory shipments.

Construction customers also bought more equipment, with end-user sales rising 20%. Backlog climbed another $6 billion sequentially to a record $78.1 billion. Backlog increased across the main segments, providing broader support than one booming application.

Unfortunately, investors wanted more from the outlook. Management maintained its mid-to-high-teens 2026 sales-growth forecast, and Q4 faces difficult comparisons. Capacity additions and delivery timing also limit near-term growth. Tariff recoveries helped quarterly profitability, so I wouldn’t extrapolate every margin improvement. Still, the combination of higher volumes and better pricing leaves me confident in the underlying performance.

Demand Can Outlast the Political Shock

Now, Wall Street seems afraid of the recent midterm outcome, but I believe Caterpillar’s demand can outlast the political shock. In power generation, available manufacturing capacity is keeping pace with growth. Management is taking some large-engine orders into 2029 and turbine orders into 2030. Customer planning agreements provide visibility beyond firm backlog. Data center operators still need reliable electricity and backup generation to use expensive computing equipment.

Further, Caterpillar is repurposing part of its Winston-Salem facility for large-engine assembly and testing. That supports plans to nearly triple large-engine capacity versus 2024 by 2030. The required factory work illustrates why supply cannot respond instantly. Expanding output should gradually convert more of today’s demand into sales.

The Democratic sweep of Congress has raised fears of tougher scrutiny. State-level resistance matters too, with moratorium advocates winning in Texas and Georgia. Delays could push Caterpillar’s deliveries back, and some projects could be canceled. My base case is more uneven scheduling and relocation, with substantial construction continuing.

The 2 GW Monarch project in West Virginia already has equipment deliveries scheduled through August 2027. Its on-site generation is designed to avoid higher bills for existing utility customers. That addresses one important source of opposition, although permitting risks remain.

The broader investment cycle also supports Caterpillar. Grid investment needs to rise roughly 50% by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). Grid construction and reshoring create work for heavy equipment. Oil and gas infrastructure needs engines and turbines, while electrification and AI infrastructure increase mineral requirements.

I should also mention that greater copper investment can support Resource Industries. Caterpillar’s installed fleet then generates aftermarket demand. Its global dealers provide parts and maintenance, helping customers avoid costly downtime. Cat Financial also makes equipment purchases easier to fund. Those relationships reinforce the brand and support repeat business.

The Sell-Off Improves the Valuation

Caterpillar’s sell-off improves the valuation considerably. Today, consensus EPS of $27.50 implies 20.13x 2026 earnings. Estimates of $32.25 for 2027 and $38.74 for 2028 imply 17.17x and 14.29x. The $46.24 forecast for 2029 reduces that to 11.97x. These forecasts imply annual EPS growth of roughly 17%, 20%, and 19%. I find that combination increasingly attractive following the decline.

I believe there is a credible reason to pay above CAT’s traditional machinery multiple. More power-generation equipment creates years of potential service work. Long-duration infrastructure projects also provide greater visibility than a normal replacement cycle. That could support a higher normalized earnings base, although Caterpillar remains cyclical.

Even at 18x 2028 consensus EPS, the shares would be worth about $697. That represents roughly 26% upside without needing the stock’s previous peak valuation. CAT’s dividend also yields about 1.1% at this price. Caterpillar also repurchased $1.2 billion of stock during Q3, helping profits accrue across fewer shares.

Those returns, of course, require orders to become profitable deliveries. Hyperscaler budgets could eventually shrink, while a construction or mining downturn would weaken equipment demand. Higher tariffs and diesel-related freight costs could squeeze margins.

Backlog growth may also moderate as factories increase output. So I would monitor delivery schedules closely. However, roughly 18x next year’s earnings leaves more room for those risks than investors had near the highs.

Is Caterpillar Stock a Buy?

Caterpillar stock has a Moderate Buy consensus, based on eight Buys and seven Holds. The average price target of $812.20 implies 46.7% upside from the recent price.

Conclusion

I remain bullish because Caterpillar’s operating momentum and production commitments support growth well beyond the current political debate. Project delays would hurt, but the infrastructure opportunity spans several industries. At a mid-to-high-teens multiple of 2028 earnings, I think the sell-off offers a compelling entry point, provided Caterpillar keeps converting demand into cash.

data.title: Reddit’s (RDDT) Short-Term Pains May Lead to Long-Term Gains
data.description:
Reddit’s (RDDT) short-term pains may lead to long-term gains, in my view. The leading social media platform lost more than 25% of its market value soon after it reported Q3 earnings on October 30. This crash followed traffic headwinds from Google’s (GOOGL) AI Overviews and the rollout of its new artificial intelligence (AI) Mode features, which negatively impacted Reddit’s user growth.

However, on November 4, Reddit stock surged 6% after the company announced that it is testing ad placements on Reddit search pages. This is a major step forward in monetizing its existing user base. The company is also planning to double down on forcing non-logged-in users to create accounts and log in to the platform. I am bullish on Reddit as I believe its recently announced strategies will trigger strong earnings growth.

Reddit Is Under Threat from AI

Although I am bullish on Reddit long term, there’s no denying the company faces a major challenge as search engines embrace AI answers. The biggest culprit is Google. The aggressive rollout of AI Overview and AI Mode have fundamentally changed SEO principles. As confirmed by Reddit’s management, Google continues to crawl Reddit to support AI answers. However, this does not translate into any user growth for Reddit.

Commenting on this during the Q3 earnings call, CEO Steven Huffman said, “Google is crawling us as hard as ever. So the demand hasn’t changed from their point of view either. The reality is: the AI Mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody as far as I know. So it’s just a fundamental shift in how Google works. It used to be a traffic driver. Now it’s not. So now that changes the equation for sure.”

Google search referrals have historically played a big role in Reddit’s user growth. The company’s user acquisition funnel usually begins with a Google query, which leads to a Reddit click, which results in a non-logged-in user acquisition. Over time, Reddit converts these users into logged-in users through its appeal. This business model is now under pressure, as AI Overview and AI Mode threaten the company’s user-acquisition funnel.

Reddit Is Doubling Down on Monetization

One of the reasons behind my bullish stance on Reddit despite the threat posed by AI is the company’s focus on improving monetization of its active users. The company is trying to achieve this objective in two ways. First, as CEO Huffman revealed on the Q3 earnings call, Reddit is gradually transitioning to a fully logged-in-only experience. The company is initially testing this in select markets outside the United States. 

The core objective of this initiative is to encourage logged-out Reddit users to create Reddit accounts and sign in to the platform. Converting its massive anonymous user base into a trackable, engaged audience should boost its monetization potential. According to company filings, Reddit served 130.3 million daily active unique users in Q3, with 76.8 million, almost 59% of total active users, using the platform without logging in. On the earnings call, Reddit confirmed that almost 80% of revenue comes from logged-in and app users (only 41% of total active users), highlighting a significant unrealized revenue opportunity.

Second, Reddit is testing direct ad placements on search pages, which is likely to improve monetization further in the long run. Reddit threads are used by high-intent users. Ads shown right within the search pages are more likely to be relevant to active users and get attention than ads in a more passive feed. If executed correctly, this strategy could help Reddit offset the negative impact of weak user growth in the foreseeable future.

AI Is Creating New Opportunities for Reddit

My bullish stance on Reddit is supported by the company’s potential to benefit from AI through content licensing agreements. Although AI search results are hurting user growth, Reddit is well positioned to monetize its massive library of user-generated questions and answers. One classic example is the company’s licensing deal with Google for $60 million per annum. This partnership gives Google real-time access to Reddit’s Data Application Programming Interface (API), allowing Google to utilize Reddit’s over 1 billion posts and 16 billion comments to train its Gemini models.

In addition to Google, OpenAI has also struck a partnership with Reddit to access its content.

Reddit’s Valuation Leaves Margin for Error

My bullish stance on Reddit is strengthened by the company’s cheap valuation. Reddit is currently valued at a forward P/E multiple of 12.16x. For comparison, social media giant Meta Platforms, Inc. (META) trades at a forward P/E multiple of 20.24x. Although Meta certainly deserves to trade at a premium to its peers given its unmatched scale and proven monetization expertise, I believe Reddit is too cheaply valued at a time when the company is beginning to double down on monetization.

In the short term, Reddit’s strategy of aggressively converting logged-out users into logged-in users is likely to create friction. This strategy may even lead to a short-term decline in active users. However, in the long term, Reddit is likely to end up with a higher monetizable user base. When this happens, Reddit’s valuation is likely to benefit, as the market will see its user base as higher-quality and authenticated, commanding premium targeted ad rates.

Is Reddit a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Based on the ratings of 24 Wall Street analysts, the average Reddit price target is $159.81, which implies upside of 70% from the current market price.

Takeaway

Reddit stock crashed following the Q3 earnings report, but gained momentum on November 4 after the company announced the rollout of ad placements in search pages. This marks a new initiative by the company to aggressively monetize its user base. Although Google’s AI search strategy threatens the company, I believe Reddit’s valuation is cheap enough to bet on it as monetization gains pace. Although short-term user growth may be disappointing, I believe Reddit is well-positioned to report strong earnings growth in the coming years. This should pave the way for a valuation re-rating.

data.title: Micron vs. Palantir: One AI Stock Is a Steal, One Is Priced for Perfection, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) sit at opposite ends of the AI trade. One makes the memory chips that AI systems can’t run without. The other sells the software that companies and governments use to put AI to work. This week, investors treated them the same way, dumping both after Democrats’ midterm sweep raised fears that the AI buildout could slow.

Thursday’s rout was severe. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, its steepest one-day drop since April 2025. Micron sank about 17.5%. Palantir lost nearly 10%, its eighth losing session in a row, which left it roughly a quarter below its October 9 record. Friday is bringing some strong relief: Micron and other chip stocks are rising in premarket trading, and Palantir is edging higher too.

Investor Julia Ostian, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, has spent months building up cash for a moment like this and has looked hard at both stocks. The investor came away with very different views of the two.

Ostian’s case for Micron rests on one idea: memory is the scarcest part of the AI supply chain. If hyperscalers trim their budgets, the investor argues, they will cut what they already have plenty of, not the part they can’t get enough of.

Micron’s latest numbers support that. Fiscal Q4 revenue jumped 379% year over year to $54.2 billion, with an adjusted gross margin of 87%. Operating cash flow came in around $44 billion in that one quarter. More than 75% of fiscal 2027 shipments are already committed. Micron also has 26 strategic customer agreements, backed by $32 billion in commitments that are mostly cash deposits, which it expects to cover more than 35% of revenue through 2030.

The 5-star investor also thinks Micron’s guidance is cautious. SK hynix’s latest quarter overlaps with the start of Micron’s current one, and it reported DRAM prices up by a high-20s percentage. By Ostian’s math, Micron’s $61.5 billion revenue guidance implies much smaller price gains. The stock trades at roughly 4x forward earnings based on consensus, and under 5x even if fiscal Q1 EPS guidance is simply multiplied by four.

The risks are familiar: price gains are slowing, and memory makers have overbuilt before. Still, at these multiples and with this much cash, Ostian rates Micron a Buy. (To watch Ostian’s track record, click here)

On the surface, Palantir’s quarter was just as impressive. Revenue rose 96% year over year to $2.31 billion, its fastest growth as a public company. U.S. commercial revenue climbed 148% to $984 million and passed U.S. government revenue for the first time. Profitability was strong too, with a 62% adjusted operating margin and a Rule of 40 score of 158%.

The problem, in Ostian’s view, is what comes next. The midpoint of Q4 guidance points to about 88% growth, down from 96%, which suggests Q3 may have been the peak. Bookings are soft too: total contract value rose just 6% YoY to $2.9 billion. Growth outside the U.S. is slow. International revenue grew 26% to about $376 million, a fraction of the U.S. pace. Palantir added 156 U.S. commercial customers over the past year. By the investor’s count, it added just six in the rest of the world.

Ostian sees a few reasons for this. Palantir’s model depends on engineers working inside client organizations, so it can’t scale like a company that just sells licenses. With U.S. demand this strong, Europe may simply not be a priority. Europe also has heavier regulation, slower AI adoption and a prickly relationship with the company. And there’s an irony in the pitch. Palantir sells sovereignty, but for many Europeans, sovereignty means relying less on American tech. The investor expects international government sales, which grew 31%, to improve first. Commercial sales abroad will likely lag for a while.

At around $159, Palantir trades near 90x its annualized Q3 earnings. That only works if earnings keep growing close to 100% a year, and the guidance points the other way. If growth cools to around 60%, Ostian notes, the stock looks expensive even after allowing for its growth. Palantir could still beat its guidance and grow into the multiple. But at today’s price, the investor sees no discount for the risks.

Accordingly, Ostian has downgraded Palantir to a Hold (i.e., Neutral), waiting for either a cheaper price or real progress in Europe.

Wall Street likes both stocks, but with a preference for the memory maker. MU is rated a Strong Buy, while its $1,621.67 average price target implies shares will gain 140% over the one-year timeframe. PLTR has a Moderate Buy consensus view, backed by a $229.09 average target, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 48%. (See MU stock forecast or PLTR stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia vs. AMD: Jim Cramer Calls One AI Chip Stock a Bargain, Says the Other Is ‘Awfully High’
data.description:
Friday morning is bringing some much-needed relief to semiconductor investors, with Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) climbing about 4% in early trading and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) jumping 8.5%. Both chipmakers are recovering from Thursday’s brutal market selloff, which sent Nvidia tumbling 9% and AMD plunging 17%, leaving investors wondering whether the latest rebound marks a buying opportunity or merely a temporary escape from further losses.

The selloff came as Wall Street grew concerned about the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure spending, particularly with political opposition threatening additional data-center construction. AMD also faced heightened scrutiny following its latest earnings report, as investors weighed the company’s enormous growth opportunities against a valuation that already assumes considerable future success.

For CNBC’s Mad Money host Jim Cramer, however, the two chip giants aren’t equally appealing at their current prices. While he believes Nvidia’s valuation has become a “bargain,” AMD’s share price still looks “awfully high” despite its outstanding quarterly performance.

But does Wall Street agree with Cramer’s assessment?

Nvidia: A Bargain, but Not Without Risks

Nvidia’s latest retreat has created a valuation that Cramer finds attractive, especially considering the company’s expected earnings growth. His argument rests on the possibility that demand for AI computing will remain strong enough to support another year of solid financial performance.

“If you think, for example, that Nvidia is going to have a good year in 2027 and just meet the current estimates set out for the company, then you’d have a stock with a growth rate of 70% that’s selling for less than 12 times next year’s earnings,” Cramer explained.

He went further, describing that combination as an “incredible, ridiculous bargain,” before reiterating his belief that Nvidia’s relatively low earnings multiple could eventually reward investors.

There is, however, an important condition attached to his enthusiasm. Cramer warned that the valuation would lose much of its appeal if restrictions on additional U.S. data centers prevented Nvidia from maintaining its growth trajectory beyond 2027.

That concern has become particularly relevant following the Democrats’ midterm election victory, which has raised the prospect of tougher permitting requirements for energy-intensive computing facilities. Nvidia’s customers continue investing heavily in AI infrastructure, but delays in building the facilities needed to house its chips could eventually affect demand.

Despite those risks, analysts remain unanimously bullish on Nvidia, awarding the stock a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 33 Buys, zero Holds, and zero Sells. The average 12-month price target stands at $322.50, implying about 71% upside from current levels. (See NVDA stock forecast)

AMD: Outstanding Earnings, But Is the Price Too High?

AMD presents Cramer with a more complicated decision, largely because the company’s financial performance has been very strong while its share price has already reflected considerable expectations.

“Perhaps the toughest to analyze is the stock of AMD,” Cramer acknowledged, describing its latest quarterly results as among the best he had ever seen.

The chipmaker’s long-term opportunity also remains enormous. During his interview with CEO Lisa Su, Cramer heard her reiterate expectations for a $1 trillion addressable market in data centers, illustrating the potential scale of demand for AMD’s processors and AI accelerators.

Yet, the veteran commentator isn’t convinced that impressive growth prospects automatically justify paying any price for the shares.

“The stock was at $188 in March. By that token, $404 seems awfully high to me. Maybe that’s the real problem,” Cramer remarked.

Thursday’s 17% plunge demonstrated how vulnerable expensive growth stocks can become when investors begin reconsidering their assumptions about future earnings. Friday’s 8% rebound suggests buyers are returning, although AMD still faces the challenge of translating its enormous addressable market into profits sufficient to justify its share price.

Wall Street appears more enthusiastic about AMD’s prospects than Cramer’s cautious remarks might suggest. The stock carries a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 26 Buys and 4 Holds, with no Sell recommendations among the 30 analysts covering the company. The average 12-month price target of $653.50 implies ~49% upside from current levels. (See AMD stock forecast)

data.title: Rocket Lab (RKLB) Still Looks Overvalued, and Q3 May Not Change That
data.description:
Rocket Lab USA (RKLB) still looks overvalued, and Q3 may not change that, in my opinion. A stock can plunge 65% and still be overvalued. That’s exactly what I see with Rocket Lab, which has lost nearly two-thirds of its value since May, even as its business continues to grow rapidly. Meanwhile, the launch of Neutron, its next-generation, medium-lift rocket, has been pushed back to 2027, while the announcement of the $8 billion Iridium (IRDM) acquisition has added another unwelcome layer of execution and dilution risks to an already expensive stock.

Now, with the “end-to-end” space company’s Q3 earnings just around the corner on November 9, the market expects revenue growth of roughly 66%. Not bad, but my concern lies elsewhere: Rocket Lab continues to burn through cash and trades at multiples that seem to assume an almost perfect future. That’s why I still don’t see the sell-off as a buying opportunity and remain bearish on RKLB.

RKLB’s Forward Valuation Still Demands Too Much Growth

Rocket Lab’s forward valuation still demands too much growth. For a high-risk, high-reward company like Rocket Lab, which operates in the highly complex space industry, grows rapidly, but still burns through cash and depends on major future projects, arguably one of the most important metrics to assess whether the recent sell-off presents a buying opportunity is forward EV/sales. After all, the company has yet to generate sustainable profits, so the question is essentially how much investors are paying for future growth.

Yet the key is to analyze how much of that growth is already priced in, rather than simply comparing the current multiple to historical levels. At present, according to the sell-side consensus, RKLB trades at 8.85x projected 2030 sales of around $3.11 billion — more than triple what is expected in 2026. This may seem attractive, but it means paying today nearly 9x the revenue the company isn’t expected to generate until four years from now.

Also note that even if Rocket Lab delivers precisely that growth, applying a still-generous 15x sales multiple in 2030 would imply a share price of approximately $78, or 70% upside from current levels, assuming a relatively stable capital structure and no further dilution.

It wouldn’t be a bad return, of course. Yet spread over four years, that would amount to roughly 14% annually. I find that return unattractive for a company with so many execution risks still ahead of it. Even stretching the multiple to 20x sales would bring us to approximately $104 per share — still well below the $150 reached in May.

Revenue Is Growing, but So Is the Cash Burn

Yet valuation is only part of the equation. Another important question is whether Rocket Lab can eventually turn its impressive revenue growth into actual cash. That’s where free cash flow margin comes in, especially for a company that still has so much expansion ahead of it.

Unfortunately for the bulls, the latest figures aren’t particularly encouraging. In Q2 2026, revenue grew 62% year-over-year to $234 million, but free cash flow burn increased from $77.4 million in Q1 to $110.1 million in Q2. That implies a free cash flow margin of roughly -47%, compared to -39% in the previous quarter. Worse still, operating cash burn also increased from $50.3 million to $84.1 million, while capex remained relatively stable.

It’s true that Rocket Lab has a strong balance sheet. The company ended Q2 with approximately $2.4 billion in cash and investments, which arguably puts it in a comfortable position to fund its expansion. However, much of that liquidity came from issuing shares. More specifically, its at-the-market (ATM) offerings alone raised about $1.53 billion in the first half of 2026, resulting in approximately 2.5% dilution.

This eases immediate concerns about funding risk, but still leaves questions about how much more cash the company will need to burn before achieving sustainable cash generation.

RKLB’s Q3 Earnings Need to Show More than Growth

That brings us to November 9, when Rocket Lab reports Q3 earnings. I’m not particularly concerned about whether the company can deliver another strong revenue figure. What matters more to me is whether that growth is finally bringing it closer to positive free cash flow, without requiring even more outside capital.

According to its latest guidance, the company expects to report revenue between $250 million and $265 million, with the midpoint close to the $257 million expected by the market. That would represent roughly 66% year-over-year growth. In other words, another quarter of extraordinary growth is already largely baked into expectations.

The problem, however, lies in profitability. Rocket Lab expects a GAAP gross margin of 29% to 31%, down from the 36.1% recorded in Q2. More concerning is that adjusted EBITDA is expected to worsen again, with a projected loss of $17 million to $23 million, compared to just $8.8 million in Q2.

It’s true that part of this pressure comes from the revenue mix and investments in Neutron. Yet that doesn’t eliminate the need to show a more convincing path toward positive cash flow.

So, rather than just looking for a potential revenue beat, I’ll be paying close attention to operating cash flow, margin trends, and, especially, management’s guidance on how much more capital will be needed before Neutron begins operations.

Is RKLB a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Wall Street has shown little skepticism toward RKLB shares. According to the RKLB forecast on TipRanks, the stock carries a Strong Buy consensus. Of the 18 analyst ratings issued over the past three months, 15 are Buy, three are Hold, and none are Sell. The average Rocket Lab price target stands at $99.19, implying a massive 115.67% upside from current levels, even after some analysts recently trimmed their targets.

Too Many Risks, Too Much Optimism Priced In

For a pre-profit space company like Rocket Lab, bumps in the road are inevitable. Yet heavy cash burn, dilution risks, and dependence on Neutron are harder to overlook now that space-stock euphoria has faded. At today’s valuation, I don’t think the potential reward justifies these risks. Q3 will need to deliver something extraordinary to change that. Until then, I see RKLB as more likely to keep sinking than soaring. I remain bearish.

data.title: Rocket Lab or CoreWeave: Cathie Wood Buys $12.7M of One Stock, Sells $18M of the Other
data.description:
Thursday’s market meltdown delivered another painful blow to high-growth stocks, with Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) tumbling about 12% and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) sinking nearly 10%. The latest selloff has pushed their year-to-date losses to approximately 34% and 39%, respectively, leaving investors wondering how much further these former market favorites could fall.

For Rocket Lab, concerns surrounding its delayed Neutron rocket and approaching earnings have added to investors’ anxiety about the company’s growth prospects. CoreWeave, meanwhile, faces growing political opposition to data-center construction following the Democrats’ midterm election victory, alongside worries about the enormous borrowing required to finance its AI infrastructure expansion.

Apparently, ARK Invest founder Cathie Wood believes a market-wide selloff doesn’t mean every beaten-down stock deserves a place in her shopping cart. On Thursday, her funds purchased 276,925 Rocket Lab shares worth about $12.7 million, while selling 412,666 CoreWeave shares valued at around $18 million.

But does Wall Street share her taste in bargains? Let’s take a closer look.

Cathie Wood Is Buying Rocket Lab Ahead of a Crucial Test

Wood’s decision to buy Rocket Lab comes at an interesting time, with the company’s third-quarter earnings scheduled for Monday, November 9. Analysts expect revenue of about $257 million, representing nearly 66% annual growth, although the aerospace manufacturer is projected to report a loss of $0.07 per share. By increasing her exposure just days before the announcement, Wood appears willing to bet that Rocket Lab’s expanding satellite operations can outweigh lingering concerns surrounding its launch plans.

The biggest concern remains Neutron, Rocket Lab’s reusable medium-lift rocket, whose inaugural flight has been postponed until 2027. Development delays have complicated its expansion plans, while the company has yet to demonstrate that Neutron can become a commercially successful launch vehicle. Nevertheless, its existing operations continue expanding, with second-quarter revenue reaching approximately $234 million and its order backlog climbing to $2.36 billion.

Overall, Wall Street remains confident about Rocket Lab’s longer-term prospects; the stock carries a Strong Buy consensus rating, supported by 15 Buys and 3 Holds. Its average 12-month price target of $99.19 suggests about 116% upside from Thursday’s closing price. (See RKLB stock forecast)

Cathie Wood Is Selling CoreWeave, but Wall Street Sees 197% Upside

Wood’s decision to sell CoreWeave comes as the Democrats’ midterm election victory raises concerns about potential restrictions on data-center construction, threatening the company’s future expansion plans. Investors are worried that stricter local regulations and rising electricity costs could interfere with planned projects, adding to the AI cloud provider’s existing financial challenges. UBS estimates that potential construction delays could affect around 30% of expected U.S. data-center capacity additions during 2028.

Financing those facilities presents another challenge, especially given CoreWeave’s dependence on borrowing to support its rapid expansion. During October, yields on certain company bonds approached 15%, illustrating how expensive additional financing could become. Such concerns matter because the provider must continue spending heavily on computing infrastructure long before collecting all the revenue associated with its customer contracts.

Yet, CoreWeave’s underlying demand remains strong. Its second-quarter revenue more than doubled from the previous year, while its contracted revenue backlog reached about $104 billion. That enormous order book offers visibility into future sales, although converting those commitments into profits requires continued investment and reliable access to financing.

Despite Wood’s decision to reduce exposure, Wall Street still sees considerable recovery potential. CoreWeave holds a Moderate Buy consensus rating, based on 22 Buys, 5 Holds, and 3 Sells. The average analyst price target stands at $129.68, implying a 197% upside from Thursday’s closing price. (See CRWV stock forecast)

data.title: 3 Quantum Computing Stocks with 130%+ Upside Potential in 2027, According to Analysts
data.description:
Quantum computing stocks offer significant upside potential in 2027, according to Wall Street analysts. Based on TipRanks data, D-Wave Quantum (QBTS), IonQ (IONQ), and Quantinuum (QNT) all carry Strong Buy consensus ratings. Their average analyst price targets imply upside of 256.05%, 133.89%, and 206.99%, respectively.

The three stocks are also rising in premarket trading on Friday after IonQ reported strong third-quarter results and raised its 2026 revenue outlook. IonQ’s revenue jumped 336% year-over-year to $173.8 million, beating Wall Street estimates. The company also lifted its full-year revenue forecast to $505 million–$515 million, well above its previous outlook. The results have lifted sentiment toward quantum computing stocks.

IonQ (IONQ)

IonQ develops quantum computers using trapped-ion technology and continues to expand its customer base. Its latest results showed strong demand, with record bookings and higher revenue expectations for 2026.

Following the results, Rosenblatt analyst John McPeake maintained a Buy rating and $70 price target. He noted that more customers are buying multiple IonQ products, signaling rising demand. McPeake also said IonQ’s $2 billion October raise gives it ample funds to expand and pursue acquisitions.

Wall Street has a Strong Buy consensus rating on $IONQ stock. The average IonQ analyst price target of $61.82 implies 133.89% upside from current levels.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS)

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) develops quantum computers and cloud services. It is expanding beyond quantum annealing into gate-model computing.

On October 1, D-Wave launched a beta program for its gate-model quantum simulator, giving select customers early access to quantum programming tools. More recently, the company delivered Italy’s first Advantage2 quantum computer under a €10 million agreement. It also extended its manufacturing partnership with SkyWater Technology, securing continued production of its superconducting chips.

Overall, QBTS carries a Strong Buy consensus rating on TipRanks. The average D-Wave Quantum analyst price target of $32.22 suggests about 256.05% upside from current levels.

Quantinuum (QNT)

Quantinuum develops quantum computers and software for businesses and researchers. Its Helios system uses trapped-ion technology and has achieved 98.9% two-qubit gate fidelity. The company plans to launch Sol in 2027, with Apollo targeted for 2029.

Morgan Stanley recently named Quantinuum its “top quantum play” and upgraded the stock to Buy. The firm lowered its price target on QNT to $62 from $78, implying 87.7% upside from current levels.

Overall, Wall Street has a Strong Buy consensus rating on $QNT stock. The average Quantinuum analyst price target of $91.55 implies 206.99% upside from current levels.
